Sampled HR@10 with 99 negatives measures success within the sampled candidate set; it can reverse model rankings relative to full-catalog evaluation, even in expectation. Preserve the pinned users, unique candidates and seed, and describe results as sampled HR@10. Repeating the identical deterministic evaluation supplies no new evidence. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) demonstrate this sampling limitation. For this benchmark, a suitable uncertainty diagnostic is a category-stratified paired user bootstrap: retain each model’s per-user hit indicator, resample the same user indices for both models within each category, then compute the equally weighted four-category mean difference. Report its 95% bootstrap interval alongside category differences. This applies the shared-index resampling documented in [SciPy’s paired bootstrap](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html). The interval estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fitted models and fixed candidate sets; it excludes training and negative-sampling variability.

Repeated hyperparameter and checkpoint selection on the same 200 users/category can overfit validation noise. [Cawley and Talbot](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) show that optimizing a finite-sample selection criterion can produce substantial selection bias. Practical safeguards here: prespecify a compact hypothesis-driven search and stopping rule, log every attempted configuration, compare candidates using paired differences, and treat small gains cautiously. Bootstrap intervals calculated after adaptive winner selection remain exploratory; they do not remove selection bias or provide selection-adjusted coverage. Keep evaluator, splits and seeds unchanged, and reserve the host’s inaccessible held-out test for the final selected model.
